title: Given weights and profits of N items and a knapsack capacity C, maximize total profit where each item can be used any number of times. Explain the Unbounded Knapsack dynamic programming pattern, how it differs from 0/1, the complexity, and a banking use case.
shortTitle: Unbounded Knapsack (Maximize Value with Unlimited Copies of Each Item)
keyPoints: Unbounded Knapsack allows each item to be chosen unlimited times, unlike 0/1 Knapsack
The 1D recurrence sweeps capacity from low to high so dp[c - w] may include the current item
The only code difference from 0/1 Knapsack is the direction of the capacity loop
Time is O(N * C) and space is O(C), same as 0/1 but with upward sweep
The pattern covers coin change, rod cutting, and ribbon cutting problems
Greedy does not always work for unbounded knapsack because value-to-weight ratios can mislead

s1_definition.oneliner: Same table as 0/1 Knapsack, but sweep capacity low to high so items can repeat.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Unbounded Knapsack** – each item may be chosen unlimited times to maximise total value within a capacity.
- **Upward sweep** – capacity loops from low to high, so `dp[c - weight]` may already include the current item, enabling reuse.
- **vs 0/1 Knapsack** – the only code difference is the loop direction; downward = use once, upward = unlimited.
- **Pattern family** – covers coin change (count ways), rod cutting, and ribbon cutting.
- **2D form** – `dp[i][c] = max(dp[i-1][c], profit[i] + dp[i][c - weight[i]])` using the same row for inclusion.
- **Complexity** – O(N * C) time and O(C) space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India offers investment instruments that Rajesh can buy repeatedly: as many units of each as he likes, up to his budget. He wants the highest total return. Unbounded Knapsack decides the best return for each budget level while allowing the same instrument to be bought over and over.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  0/1 vs Unbounded Knapsack: Sweep Direction
  ───────────────────────────────────────────

  0/1 Knapsack (each item once):
  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
  │  for each item:                  │
  │    c = capacity → weight[i]      │
  │    dp[c] = max(dp[c], v+dp[c-w]) │
  │    ◄──── sweep direction ◄────   │
  │    dp[c-w] = OLD (previous item) │
  └─────────────────────────────────┘

  Unbounded Knapsack (unlimited copies):
  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
  │  for each item:                  │
  │    c = weight[i] → capacity      │
  │    dp[c] = max(dp[c], v+dp[c-w]) │
  │    ────► sweep direction ────►   │
  │    dp[c-w] = NEW (current item)  │
  └─────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Unbounded Knapsack is the repetition variant of the knapsack problem, where each item can be chosen as many times as you like. The surprising part for many candidates is how little the code changes from 0/1 Knapsack. The single meaningful difference is the direction of the capacity sweep in the one-dimensional form.

In 0/1 Knapsack, the capacity loop runs from high to low so that dp[c - weight] holds the value from the previous item. In Unbounded Knapsack, the loop runs from low to high so that dp[c - weight] may already include a copy of the current item, which is what enables repetition. The loop direction is the correctness lever, not a stylistic choice.

At the National Bank of India, Rajesh used this in an advisory engine for instruments that customers could buy in unlimited units, each with a unit cost and a unit return, to maximise total return within a budget. The upward capacity sweep allowed the same instrument to be selected multiple times.

The pattern covers coin change, rod cutting, and ribbon cutting problems. A senior engineer knows that for counting problems the loop order (items outer vs capacity outer) determines combinations versus permutations, which is a separate but related subtlety.

Remember one sentence: Unbounded Knapsack is the same DP as 0/1 but with an upward capacity sweep that deliberately allows item reuse.
